Hi, I'm Misha. I'm a UI engineer at Netflix. My team builds tools for content analysis. To put it simply, we detect scary and grown up stuff - to make sure shows like Squid Game or Stranger Things are recommended to you - and not to your little kids.

These days, I also spend a lot of time on developer productivity - helping to increase AI adoption across Netflix teams.

But I'm not going to talk about AI today. Well… a bit.
Instead, I want to show you how our product team adopted Netflix UI platform tooling - with real-life examples and learnings you can easily apply at your job.

To set some context, let me tell you about Netflix UI Platform. What’s that and why we need it?
Let’s imagine you’d like to watch something on Netflix. For example, Squid Game. Anyone here watched Squid Game? You search for it, you find it, there it is.

But, before a movie is ready to play, it goes through a long journey.
It starts with a screenplay. Then, deals are signed - with actors, directors, writers.
Financials are handled.
The movie is produced.
Promoted.
Localized.
Age rated.

And that's just the surface. There are hundreds of internal tools that power this process.

You’ve also probably heard a bit about Netflix culture. Iterate fast, run experiments, innovate, don’t let processes or bureaucracy stop you.

To be successful, the business needs to balance that off with quality, consistency, multi-device support.
These two groups don’t always match.

Netflix's answer to that mismatch is platform tooling. Shared tools and libraries that help ship fast without sacrificing quality.

On the Web UI side, we call those UIPR. UI Paved Road.

Spoiler alert: that paved road has some bumps.

Why migrate to platform tooling at all?

Every codebase grows in complexity over time, right? But when you migrate to platform tooling... a big chunk of that complexity goes away. You're no longer maintaining custom solutions. Complexity and maintenance drop. Onboarding gets easier.

And everything else goes up: reliability, productivity, consistency, security. Because the platform team handles those concerns for you, across all apps.

Before UIPR and platform creation, every Netflix team picked tools that worked best for them. Which meant every team picked something different.

Here are all JS bundlers which were used across the apps. React-scripts, vite, webpack, gulp... has anyone here heard of craco/craco? Yeah.

And it wasn't just bundlers. Same story for styles, feature flagging, telemetry, localization.

How did the platform team go from 8 different bundlers to one paved road recommendation? Three phases.

First, analyze. Look at what hundreds of apps are using. What can be shared. What is app-specific.
Second, select. Explore the options, find what works best, document it, maintain it as a platform.
Third, bundle. Package everything into a single framework so teams can adopt it in one click.
UIPR stands on two pillars. Web Framework. Hawkins Design System.
Let me show you what Web Framework adoption looked like for our team.

Here's a very simplified version of one of our apps. It has a movie search component and a user menu in the header.

From the architectural standpoint, it’s a monorepo app, which depends on two reusable packages: movie-search and user-menu.

Looks simple, right? It's not. Because it’s not using UIPR platform tools yet.

Instead, the app and packages depend on another package called Application Provider. It handles integration with internal system and provides shared infrastructure tools like a configured GraphQL client, feature flags, telemetry and more. Application Provider pulls those from other custom packages - all living in the same monorepo.

A monorepo of around 50 packages and 10 apps that our org owns.

On top of that, there is a community layer. Libraries for auth, logging, and more - maintained by entire Netflix Enterprise community. And each app has its own configs and code generation logic. That's the legacy setup we inherited.

If you look closer, a big portion of this can be reused across apps. Most apps need the same things: auth, error handling, feature flags, telemetry. TypeScript, ESLint, and Vite default configs. So this must be provided by UIPR platform.

And it is. All of these indeed have UIPR equivalents now. We no longer need to maintain custom alternatives in our monorepo. The monorepo is much leaner.
Now, Application Provider can pull from platform directly.
And distribute the capabilities to our apps and packages.
But wait, if Application Provider is just an orchestrator of platform libs... it must be maintained by the platform, too. Yes - that’s exactly how Web Framework was born.

Now we don’t need Application Provider. Now our app just needs to plug into Web Framework entrypoint and get all the tooling out of the box. No more custom infrastructure packages cluttering the monorepo. The app just handles business logic - and nothing else. NOW, it’s simpler, right?

So, Web Framework gives you this enterprise-ready pre-configured app setup out of the box. All of that managed by the platform team.
The platform team also keeps your dependencies up-to-date for you.

Now you can see how Web Framework was born and why it became the migration goal for Netflix's internal apps.
But our team was one of the first to migrate. We did not want to end up like this guy. So we had to figure out the process for that.

Our first approach: Big Bang Migration. Replace Application Provider with Web Framework, across all apps and packages at once.

Sounds ambitious! Quick question. Who's tried a big bang migration like this? … and succeeded? Yeah, so you probably know where this is going…

The app and packages all depend on Application Provider.
Then, just swap those dependencies to Web Framework, right?
But there's another app in the monorepo. It also pulls in Application Provider and the same re-usable packages. And you can't have both in the same monorepo. Web Framework and Application Provider conflict because they configure the same tools. So you need to migrate that app too.
And then the rest. You can’t migrate one app without migrating them all. It’s like a snowball.

And that’s the actual dependency graph of our monorepo at that point.
That little thing in the center is Application Provider which we’re trying to replace.

During the big bang migration, the problems piled up.
Tight coupling - apps and packages depend on the same things. You can't migrate one app without migrating all of them. And you can't verify everything works until everything is done.
Bugs everywhere - it’s impossible to reliably catch regressions across all apps after every change you make.
Incompatible features - Vite, React Router and many other libs needed upgrades first, to meet Web Framework requirements.
Missing features - some very specific things Web Framework didn't cover at all.
Cross-team coordination - every team in the monorepo had to complete it’s part of the migration. And we couldn't finish until they all did.
Frequent rebasing - to stay in sync with main. Because product work was happening alongside.
And the cherry on top: a million-line diff. Impossible to review.
Big bang migration failed.

To be fair, it had some pros. You need to do it just once, and everyone benefits. It’s a focused effort you can track. And it highlighted all of the blockers we had.

But the bottom line: there's no room for error. One blocker stops everything, teams have to wait for each other, and regressions are hard to catch.

We dropped this effort.

Instead, we went with the second approach: phased migration. We split one big effort into three phases: preparation, the migration itself, and follow-ups. Also, we pinned dependencies per app, so Web Framework and Application Provider can temporarily co-exist in one monorepo. That solved dependency conflicts and unblocked migrating apps one-by-one.
Start with one pioneer app to figure out the process and estimate effort. Then replicate it to the second one. Then the next, And if one fails, it doesn't block the rest.

With this approach, there is much more green than red.

You get flexibility, white-glove platform support, and each step is small enough to review and verify. The pioneer app becomes a blueprint for everyone else.

Of course, it has some tradeoffs, too. Some apps lag behind, and the monorepo is a bit messy until every team completes the migration - multiple versions of the same library are pulled in.

We decided: that’s the way to go.

Here's the phased approach in practice. If you can’t see everything here from where you’re sitting, that’s exactly the point. Instead of one massive effort, we now have this long list of small, independent tasks. Same runbook for every app. Each phase (preparation, migration, follow-ups) can be done separately, with items parallelized, and verified on their own.

And once you've documented this process for one app: this high-level plan, the step-by-step guides, the PRs. You can give that runbook to your most hardworking teammate.
The one that never complains about rebasing.

Some outcomes of the phased approach.

- We went from two months for the pioneer app migration to under a week for every app after it. The reason is how well we documented the process, and how easy it was to follow.
- In fact, we turned those docs and artifacts into an agent skill - so an AI agent can run the migration end-to-end: from preparing the app to visual regression checks.
- The docs and the skill turned out useful not just for our monorepo, but for many others across the company, and the skill was graduated to the platform itself.

What we learned from the process:

Divide and conquer. Big bang failed under its own weight. So, it’s better to ship one small item at a time.
Fail fast, adapt faster. Big bang failed, but it exposed every blocker, and helped to shape approach #2.
Collaborate with the platform. We gave early feedback. Bugs got fixed before anyone else hit them. Our edge cases shaped the framework for everyone.
Leave a runbook. Step-by-step guides. Decision log. Pull requests. So that everyone can follow that runbook. Including the agents.
Now the second pillar of UI Paved Road: Hawkins - Netflix in-house design system.
Hawkins is the building blocks: components, forms, tables, guidelines, usage metrics. All built with performance, accessibility, and consistency in mind.

One of the challenges we faced with Hawkins, was the new table component adoption. Here's a table inside one of our apps.

It’s implemented using hawkins-table component. Which is built on top of a third-party library: React Data Grid.
By the way, raise your hand if you've heard of React Data Grid. [if few hands]: "A few of you." [if many hands]: "Oh, more than I expected. Veteran crowd."

Now, raise your hand if you've heard of AG Grid. [if many]: "Many more. Right." [if few]: "Niche crowd today."
AG Grid is one of the most popular JS table libraries. It has more features, better performance. So hawkins team selected it as the foundation for the next version of the table component. They're calling the component hawkins-table-next.

Well, that’s what they told us they were doing. Because that new component is not released yet. Still under development.

So, as a product team, how do we ship new features then? We need to make a decision: use the old table component, ship features now.
Or wait for the new table component, and ship features later.
Old table: no delay, familiar APIs. But you're knowingly creating tech debt.
New table: has more features, no tech debt. But it delays product work. And there's a learning curve.

Team Old Table raise your hand.
Now, Team New Table, raise your hand.

Neither option is great. So we found a third way.

Step one: use AG Grid directly. Don't wait for hawkins-table-next, start building with AG Grid APIs now. Ship product work on time.

Step two: Swap with hawkins-table-next once it’s released. Since it wraps AG Grid under the hood, you're already using the right APIs. The swap is minimal.

Step three: gradually migrate the other tables across the app. Until you have no references to the old table.

So, what we did was using future APIs, future foundation directly:
Adopt the future platform direction before the official platform tool is ready.

The wins: no delay in product work, less tech debt to clean up later, and you get early feedback on new APIs.
The trade-offs: there's a learning curve upfront, you need some initial styling and licencing workarounds, and there's cleanup after the final swap. But compared to the alternatives - it's a much better way to go.

Only do this when:
1. The platform direction is public, durable, and specific.
Public: The platform team has communicated the future direction.
Durable: The vendor or foundation is unlikely to change mid-flight.
Specific: You know enough to build toward the same API surface.

2. Finalized platform APIs will be similar to the foundation’s API that you adopted.
In our example, we knew that the new component is mostly a wrapper for existing APIs with integration into Netflix ecosystem. So we knew exactly that if we start using existing APIs, it would be easy to swap packages.

What we learned from the process:

Align direction, not timing. You can't always wait for the platform. But if you're moving the same way, you'll eventually meet at one point.
Product work is non-negotiable. Your stakeholders should never care about such migrations. Product work must be delivered on time.
Give early feedback. Our feedback shaped table-next. With this early adoption, we were also helping build the final solution.

In the first two approaches, we knew where the platform was going. Hawkins had chosen AG Grid, and the web framework already existed with with capabilities ready to replace our custom solutions.

In this section 3, we only know that a platform solution is coming. We don’t know what its API will look like. For that level of uncertainty, we use Ports and Adapters approach.

Ports & Adapters is an architectural pattern that helps you keep the domain logic independent of specific external APIs.

Let’s go through an example. This is a movie cards layout from one of our apps. Each shows a title and a movie summary.
Except the third one. That title came to us from outside our own catalogue and it arrived without a summary, which happens quite often.

We have AI now, so we can generate the summary. The question is how do you integrate with AI? AI landscape is moving very fast. So platform AI implementations change often, too. Newer AI implementations appear every month. That’s exactly what Ports & Adapters help to solve.
This is Ports & Adapters architecture. Let’s go deep into it. It has four parts.
Display renders.
Core owns the business rules.
Ports are feature-owned interfaces.
Adapters are external integrations. They connect your feature to external systems like GraphQL, notifications, permissions.

Now look at the arrows. Core depends on interfaces, not on concrete adapter implementations. The adapters implement those interfaces. If the notification API changes next month, Core stays intact.
The display side works the same way. Display depends on the interface implemented by Core instead of depending on the core directly.

This dotted box marks the domain boundary. The Core and the interfaces are inside. Display and adapters are outside.
Dependencies point inward, so React, GraphQL, platform APIs and other external internal integrations stay outside of the domain. This also means that the domain knows nothing about the external infrastructure. This is the dependency inversion principle in action.

This is the same diagram with code attached. It’s how we implemented movie summary logic from my earlier example.
Don’t worry if you can’t read it fully. I’ll zoom in in a second.

Let’s start in the middle - with the business domain. The feature owns both interfaces/ports. The left one (UseMovieSummaryCore interface) describes what Core exposes to Display. It’s just the summary string in this example. The right one (ForFetchingGeneratedMovieSummary interface) describes what Core needs from an integration and the signature that this integration needs to follow.

Core itself requests the generated summary through that interface, then applies a business rule: use the catalogue summary when it exists; otherwise use the generated one.
Display consumes the contract exposed by Core. It receives a summary string and renders it. It doesn’t know and doesn’t care whether the summary came from the catalog or was generated by AI.

On the other side, the adapter implements the interface Core depends on. It receives the movie ID and returns generated AI summary string.
As you can seem, the exact platform integration, LLM model and API response shape are contained within the adapter and stay outside the domain.
That’s it for the example. But not for the pattern.

Besides getting us a good degree of separation of concerns, Ports & Adapters makes the Core logic straightforward to test.

By passing in mock adapters, and testing on the Core itself rather than on the DOM, we get a few benefits:
- Tests are faster since we don’t have to render any complex UI components or go through the network layer.
- Tests are easier to write since there are no technology-specific concerns, such as rendering, context providers, etc.
- Tests are resilient to technology changes. If we make a technology-specific decision, we only need to switch up or tweak an Adapter or the Display, while the Core and its tests remain intact.

All four wins here come from separating what the feature does from how it integrates with external systems - because these are things that change for completely different reasons. What the feature does is dictated by product requirements. How it integrates with external systems is dictated by those external APIs, like platform APIs.

On the other hand, boilerplate is real. Defining interfaces, adapters, mock builders, for something that can be a single function call. Sometimes it’s an overkill.
Indirection causes pain, too. Especially when debugging. Someone new wants to know where the summary comes from and they can't follow a single call. Display, interface, core, another interface, adapter, and only then the network call. Five places to check instead of just one function call.

Use Ports and Adapters when the integration API is volatile. AI is a great example of such volatility.
Also when you simply don’t know what the integrations will look like.
And when business logic should remain independent of integrations.

As a bonus, Ports and Adapters is a good fit for an agent skill because it defines boundaries and intentions very clearly. The agent doesn’t have to guess where code belongs.
Write those rules into SKILL.md: where business logic goes, how interfaces and adapters are named, which signatures they follow. What tests should cover and how to build adapter mocks.
Rules are not always enough, so include a reference to an example feature you implemented with this appproach in the past. The example will make agent output much more consistent.
You can then use the skill both for building features and reviewing code against it.

BTW, this pattern isn’t specific to Netflix. However, we’ve adapted it pretty well for building UIs with React. The React Ports & Adapters agent skill is open-sourced. Check it out on GitHub.

What did we learn from this?

The feature and the integrations change for different reasons. A platform change shouldn’t force us to rewrite the business rules.
It costs extra code, so I only use it where you’re ready to pay the boilerplate cost.
And finally, it’s relatively easy to automate with AI and make the output consistent.

I’ve shown two absolutely different examples of adopting things:
- one by using the foundation directly - when you know what that foundation will be in the future;
- and another is by using Ports & Adapters - when you don’t know which APIs will be used, but you know which capability you will need.

Different approaches, but the same intent - keep shipping while moving toward the platform’s future direction.

The important thing is that any approach you take when pioneering something always leads to an early feedback loop - which turns your product teams into design partners for the platform.

This is what it looks like: product team adopts some early platform solution. It spots gaps early. Platform adjusts according to the feedback and releases a better solution. The loop starts over.

So next time you're waiting for the perfect tool to drop, start with what you have. Be the pioneer. Adopt early. And pave the road yourself.
